To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) cannabis use is associated with alterations in neural systems that mediate reward, cognition, emotion and stress responsivity; 2) cannabis use in adolescence and vulnerable populations, including those with psychiatric disorders, is associated with an increased risk of CUD; and 3) the neurobiology of CUD shares common characteristics with other substance-use disorders, and may be associated with a distinct neurobiology that is related to the specific pharmacologic properties of cannabis.

(i) cannabis use is associated with changes in brain structure, neurochemistry and function that are associated with CUD; (ii) cannabis use is also associated with changes in neurocognitive function, and (iii) the effects of cannabis use and CUD are modulated by sex, genetic factors and environmental factors.

(a) cannabis use disorder is associated with alterations in neural systems that regulate reward, stress responsivity and cognition and (b) cannabis use disorder shares common neural characteristics with substance use disorders in general, which could inform the development of novel treatment strategies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the neurobiological mechanisms of cannabis use disorder (e.g. cannabis addiction) in humans, and the development of new treatments for cannabis use disorder.
identifying the neurobiological mechanisms that contribute to the development of cannabis use disorder and the potential for cannabis to be used to treat other psychiatric illnesses.
the development of Cud, its neurobiological correlates and the potential for pharmacotherapy to reduce the burden of CUD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cannabis use is associated with changes in brain structure and function, and that these changes are related to the use of cannabis.
CUD is a heterogeneous condition, which can be associated with a variety of clinical symptoms, which may or may not be related to cannabis use.

cannabis use disorder is associated with a complex interplay between environmental and genetic factors, which can be modulated by the endocannabinoid system, and that the development of CUID is associated with a disruption of the balance between the endocannabinergic system and other neurotransmitter systems, such as dopamine, serotonin and glutamate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

cannabis use disorder is associated with alterations in brain function, structure, and connectivity that may be related to the development and maintenance of the disorder and that are shared with other substance use and psychiatric disorders.
CUD is a clinical syndrome with a neurobiological basis.
cannabis is not as safe as it has been perceived to be and that the neurobiology of CUD is similar to other substance use disorders and is associated with psychiatric comorbidities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cannabis use disorder is not just a disorder of the brain but rather a disorder of the entire person, and as such, a comprehensive approach to treatment is required.

CUD is a complex disorder with many contributing factors that may be modulated by genetic and environmental factors, and that the neurobiological systems underlying CUD share common characteristics with other substance abuse disorders.
CUD is associated with alterations of the endocannabinoid system and its interaction with other neurobiological systems that mediate reward, stress responsivity, and cognitive control.
